intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome (ABERS) is caused by mutation in the TBX22 gene (300307) on chromosome Xq21.1.

checks.claim: Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome (ABERS) is caused by mutation in the TBX22 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: most importantly confirms that TBX22 is the gene underlying Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome

checks.claim: The TBX22 gene is located on chromosome Xq21.1.
checks.evidence_quote: X-linked cleft palate (CPX) is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the TBX22 transcription factor
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give a band, but Xq21.1 is TBX22's standard chromosomal location, which the rules count as supported.

paragraphs.text: Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome is a CHARGE-like disorder. Its features are cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radial synostosis (Abruzzo and Erickson, 1977). The disorder is X-linked and results from a splicing mutation in the TBX22 gene (Pauws et al., 2013).

checks.claim: Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome is a CHARGE-like disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: a family with X-linked, CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome, of unknown etiology

checks.claim: Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome features cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radial synostosis.
checks.evidence_quote: A new syndrome characterized by cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radial synostosis has been described.
checks.explanation: The abstract lists exactly these six features.

checks.claim: Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome is X-linked.
checks.evidence_quote: a family with X-linked, CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome, of unknown etiology

checks.claim: Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome results from a splicing mutation in the TBX22 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: X-linked CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome and classic cleft palate with ankyloglossia result from TBX22 splicing mutations.

paragraphs.text: Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) described a family with a new syndrome of cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radial synostosis.

checks.claim: Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) described a family with a new syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: The family history suggests either an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance with limited expression in females or X-linkage.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports a new syndrome and analyses its family history for an inheritance pattern, which means a family was described. It never uses the words 'a family', but this follows directly.

checks.claim: The syndrome in the family described by Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) consisted of cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radial synostosis.
checks.evidence_quote: A new syndrome characterized by cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radial synostosis has been described.
checks.explanation: The features match those in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) carried out a follow-up study of the family they had reported earlier. They wanted to see how the patients had developed since the first report and to find out whether they had CHARGE syndrome. Other reports had cited this family as an example of familial CHARGE syndrome. After the follow-up, Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) concluded that the patients did not have familial CHARGE syndrome or the CHARGE association.

checks.claim: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) carried out a follow-up study of the family they had previously reported.
checks.evidence_quote: Therefore, we decided to do a follow-up study on this family to assess the subsequent development of the patients and to determine if they have the CHARGE syndrome.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes a follow-up study of the family the authors had reported before.

checks.claim: The aim of the Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) follow-up study was to see how the patients had developed since the first report and to find out whether they had CHARGE syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: we decided to do a follow-up study on this family to assess the subsequent development of the patients and to determine if they have the CHARGE syndrome.
checks.explanation: The abstract states both aims of the study.

checks.claim: Other reports had cited the Abruzzo-Erickson family as an example of familial CHARGE syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: This family has been cited in several reports as an example of familial CHARGE syndrome.

checks.claim: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) concluded that the patients in their family did not have familial CHARGE syndrome or the CHARGE association.
checks.evidence_quote: We do not think that the patients in this family have the Charge syndrome or association.
checks.explanation: The formal conclusion ('We conclude that our patients do not have familial CHARGE syndrome') mentions only the syndrome. 'Association' appears only in the authors' earlier stated opinion, not in the conclusion.

paragraphs.text: Pauws et al. (2013) noted that the phenotype in the family with X-linked CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome went beyond classic X-linked cleft palate (CPX) to include sensorineural deafness and coloboma. These features had not been reported before in CPX patients, but they were consistent with the developmental expression pattern of Tbx22.

checks.claim: Pauws et al. (2013) noted that the phenotype in the family with X-linked CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome went beyond classic X-linked cleft palate (CPX) to include sensorineural deafness and coloboma.
checks.evidence_quote: The phenotype extends to additional features including sensorineural deafness and coloboma, which are suggested by the Tbx22 developmental expression pattern but not previously associated in CPX patients.

checks.claim: Sensorineural deafness and coloboma had not been reported before in patients with X-linked cleft palate (CPX).
checks.evidence_quote: The phenotype extends to additional features including sensorineural deafness and coloboma, which are suggested by the Tbx22 developmental expression pattern but not previously associated in CPX patients.

checks.claim: The sensorineural deafness and coloboma in the Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome family were consistent with the developmental expression pattern of Tbx22.
checks.evidence_quote: The phenotype extends to additional features including sensorineural deafness and coloboma, which are suggested by the Tbx22 developmental expression pattern but not previously associated in CPX patients.

paragraphs.text: Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) concluded that the family history fit either autosomal dominant inheritance with limited expression in females or X-linked inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Pauws et al. (2013) found that a TBX22 mutation segregated with the phenotype in the family, which they described as having X-linked CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome.

checks.claim: Pauws et al. (2013) found that a TBX22 mutation segregated with the phenotype in the family with X-linked CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: A novel TBX22 splice acceptor mutation (c.593-5T>A) was identified that tracked with the phenotype in this family.
checks.explanation: 'Tracked with the phenotype' means the same as 'segregated with'.

paragraphs.text: Pauws et al. (2013) studied a family with X-linked CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome of unknown cause. They found a novel splice acceptor mutation in the TBX22 gene (c.593-5T-A) that segregated with the phenotype. In silico analysis predicted that the variant abolishes normal mRNA splicing. An in vitro splicing assay suggested that alternative splice sites were likely to be used. The authors concluded that TBX22 is the gene underlying Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome.

checks.evidence_quote: This study hypothesized a possible involvement of TBX22 in a family with X-linked, CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome, of unknown etiology.

checks.claim: Pauws et al. (2013) found a novel splice acceptor mutation in the TBX22 gene (c.593-5T-A) in the Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome family.
checks.evidence_quote: A novel TBX22 splice acceptor mutation (c.593-5T>A) was identified that tracked with the phenotype in this family.

checks.evidence_quote: A novel TBX22 splice acceptor mutation (c.593-5T>A) was identified that tracked with the phenotype in this family.

checks.claim: In silico analysis predicted that the TBX22 c.593-5T-A variant abolishes normal mRNA splicing.
checks.evidence_quote: All three variants were predicted to abolish normal mRNA splicing
checks.explanation: The c.593-5T>A variant is one of the three variants predicted to abolish normal splicing.

checks.claim: An in vitro splicing assay suggested that alternative splice sites were likely to be used with the TBX22 c.593-5T-A variant.
checks.evidence_quote: an in vitro assay indicated that use of alternative splice sites was a likely outcome

checks.claim: Pauws et al. (2013) concluded that TBX22 is the gene underlying Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Pauws et al. (2013) also studied patients with classic X-linked cleft palate. In these patients they found 2 TBX22 splice donor variants in the same exon as the Abruzzo-Erickson mutation: a novel c.767+5G-A variant and a previously known canonical c.767+1G-A mutation. In silico and in vitro splicing studies predicted that both variants disrupt normal splicing.

paragraphs.text: In the differential diagnosis with CHARGE syndrome: Davenport et al. (1986) described the external ear anomalies of CHARGE syndrome. The pinnae were short and wide, and often cupped and asymmetric. Other features were a distinctive triangular concha, a break between the antihelix and antitragus, and 'snipped-off' portions of the helical folds. The authors stated that these patterns were distinctive enough that a preliminary diagnosis of CHARGE syndrome could often be made from ear shape alone.

paragraphs.text: Metlay et al. (1987) reported a boy with CHARGE syndrome. He had a coloboma of the optic nerve head and a congenital heart defect consisting of atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, and parachute mitral valve. He also had choanal atresia, severe growth retardation, genital hypoplasia, abnormal ears, cleft lip and palate, and pectus carinatum. His chromosomes were normal. He died at 19 months of age, and autopsy findings were reported. His mother was short and had hearing impairment, choanal atresia, and a coloboma. Metlay et al. (1987) took this as evidence of dominant transmission of the disorder in this family, and they reviewed other familial cases from the literature.
